reasoning:
The claim that MSG causes headaches, numbness, and other symptoms associated with "Chinese restaurant syndrome" is false and has been debunked by scientific consensus. 

The term "Chinese restaurant syndrome" originated from a single letter written to the New England Journal of Medicine in 1968, which speculated on the cause of post-meal symptoms. Since then, numerous rigorous, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies have failed to establish any reliable causal link between monosodium glutamate (MSG) and these symptoms when consumed in normal dietary amounts. 

Both the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the World Health Organization (WHO) classify MSG as "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS). Chemically, the glutamate in MSG is identical to the natural glutamate found in foods like tomatoes, cheese, and mushrooms, which do not trigger such reactions. While a very small subset of the population might exhibit transient, mild sensitivity when consuming massive doses (3 grams or more) of MSG on an empty stomach without food, MSG does not cause these symptoms under normal eating conditions.
